summary: Defines an architecture and framework for a GMPLS control plane for Ethernet used as a transport network technology, in roles once held by SONET/SDH, TDM and ATM. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo applies the GMPLS control plane, which sets up labelled paths with reserved bandwidth, to Ethernet. It explains which parts of the existing GMPLS machinery can be reused as they are, and which parts need new values for Ethernet's different ways of forwarding frames.

questions: how does gmpls control ethernet forwarding
subtitle: How the GMPLS control plane can be applied to Ethernet transport networks.

tldr.problem: Ethernet is being used for transport work that used to be done with SONET, TDM or ATM, but the IEEE and ITU-T work on Ethernet has produced forwarding and management extensions without an explicitly routed, constraint-based control plane.
tldr.mechanism: The document applies the GMPLS control plane to Ethernet, defines an Ethernet label switched path, and maps the various Ethernet switching types onto it, using the existing GMPLS routing, signalling and link management as far as possible.
tldr.outcome: The document is a framework: it defines no label format and no signalling, and leaves those to technology-specific documents, with the switching type and interface capability values still to be defined.

facts.label: Control plane addressing
facts.value: IP addresses, with numbered and unnumbered interfaces

facts.label: Path computation options
facts.value: Distributed, on a management station, or on a path computation server

today: RFC 5828 is an Informational document published by the IETF in March 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a framework: it defines no label format and no signalling of its own, and leaves those to technology-specific documents that build on it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
There has been significant recent work on increasing the capabilities of Ethernet switches, and as a result the role of Ethernet is rapidly expanding into transport networks that used to belong to technologies such as SONET/SDH, time division multiplexing and ATM. The development of Ethernet capabilities for these areas is active and ongoing.

Several organisations have been extending Ethernet for transport networks: the IEEE 802.1 Working Group, the ITU-T and the Metro Ethernet Forum. They have focused on Ethernet forwarding, on management plane extensions and on the Ethernet spanning tree control plane, but not on an explicitly routed, constraint-based control plane. Forwarding-plane extensions have been defined for different transport Ethernet forwarding models, protection modes and service interfaces, including IEEE 802.1ah, IEEE 802.1Qay, ITU-T G.8011 and MEF 6. These give the forwarding plane more flexibility and in some cases allow a departure from forwarding based on a spanning tree: 802.1ah does so by adding a provider address space, and 802.1Qay supports provisioning systems and network control protocols that explicitly select traffic-engineered paths.

This document provides a framework for GMPLS Ethernet Label Switching, which will likely need more than one switching type to support the different models. Because the GMPLS procedures that must be extended depend on the switching type, those extensions are left to technology-specific documents.

It also sets out the Ethernet formats that matter. In the provider bridge model developed by the IEEE 802.1ad project and amended into IEEE 802.1Q, an extra VLAN identifier is added; that identifier is the Service VID, carried in a Service TAG. In Provider Backbone Bridges, a Backbone VID and a B-MAC header with a service instance, the I-TAG, encapsulate a customer Ethernet frame or a service Ethernet frame.

The Ethernet forwarding plane and management plane extensions allow the standard Spanning Tree Protocols to be disabled, but they do not define an explicitly routed, constraint-based control plane. The IETF's GMPLS work provides a common control plane for different data plane technologies, and the GMPLS architecture of RFC 3945 can be applied to Ethernet as well as to optical and TDM networks. This document provides a framework for using GMPLS to control transport Ethernet label switched paths, and it is the data plane aspects of those paths that are outside its scope.

The intent is to reuse and stay aligned with as much of the GMPLS protocol set as possible. Reusing the IP control plane addressing allows the existing signalling, routing, Link Management Protocol and path computation to be used as they are. The GMPLS protocols support hierarchical and contiguous paths, and support network reference points from user-network interfaces to network-network interfaces. Additions to the existing GMPLS capabilities will only be made to accommodate features unique to transport Ethernet.
sections.plainLanguage: Ethernet already knows how to forward frames well, but it has no way to say that a particular path must have a given amount of bandwidth and avoid certain links. GMPLS is the machinery that does that for other technologies, and the memo is about pointing it at Ethernet.

sections.title: Ethernet Switching Types and OAM
sections.content:
In Ethernet switching terminology the bridge relay is responsible for forwarding and replicating frames, and it forwards on the Ethernet header fields: the VLAN identifier and the destination MAC address. Provider Backbone Bridges have also introduced a service instance tag, the I-TAG. Across the Ethernet extensions, several forwarding functions or service interfaces have been defined using combinations of VLAN identifiers, destination MAC addresses and I-TAGs.

The switching types are port based, S-tagged and I-tagged. Port based is a frame-based service that supports specific frame types, with no service VLAN tagging and no MAC-address-based switching. S-tagged services come in several forms. In the one-to-one service, each VLAN identifier is mapped into a different service. Bundled S-tagged service supports mapping multiple identifiers into a single service, in the many-to-one form where several identifiers map into the same service and the all-to-one form where all identifiers map into the same service, with transparent as a special case in which all frames are mapped from a single incoming port to a single destination Ethernet port. In the I-tagged service type, the edge of a provider backbone network consists of a combined backbone relay and service instance relay. An I-TAG contains a service identifier, a 24-bit I-SID, and priority markings as well as other fields, and an I-tagged service is typically between the edges of the network and terminated at each edge on a component that faces a customer port, so the service is often not visible except at the edges.

The switching types determine which header fields the forwarding function uses, for example the VLAN identifier alone or the identifier together with destination MAC addresses, and a switching type may also require extra Ethernet headers or fields. In most bridging cases the header fields cannot be changed, though some translation of VLAN identifier values is permitted, typically at the network edges. Across all service types the Ethernet data plane is bidirectional congruent: the forward and reverse paths share exactly the same set of nodes, ports and bidirectional links. The document calls this property fundamental, and notes that the 802.1 group has maintained it in the definition of Connectivity Fault Management, which is part of the overall operations capability.

Operations, administration and maintenance messages rely on data-plane forwarding in both directions, so finding a broken path or a misdirected packet depends on those messages following the path. Because their identifiers depend on the data plane, they work equally well for provisioned or GMPLS-controlled paths. Ethernet operations currently consist of the continuity check message and remote defect indication, loopback message and reply, link trace message and reply, and vendor-specific message and reply, all defined in both IEEE 802.1ag and ITU-T Y.1731, plus, in Y.1731, the alarm indication signal, locked signal, test, loss measurement message and reply, delay measurement and its message and reply, experimental message and reply, and automatic protection switching with a maintenance communication channel.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of Ethernet service and each forwards frames on different header fields. Whatever the kind, the forward and reverse directions use exactly the same nodes and links, which is a property the framework depends on.

sections.title: The GMPLS Ethernet Framework
sections.content:
The GMPLS architecture allows a control plane to be applied to a technology by controlling the data-plane and switching characteristics of that technology, and it allows control of Ethernet bridges and other Layer 2 technologies using the Layer-2 Switch Capable switching type, although the control of Ethernet switching was never explicitly defined in the GMPLS signalling or routing documents. A clear separation between control plane and data plane lets the control plane stay unchanged while controlling different technologies, and the architecture requires IP connectivity for the control plane but does not otherwise require an IP data plane.

All aspects of GMPLS, addressing, signalling, routing and link management, may be applied to Ethernet switching, and GMPLS can provide control for traffic-engineered and protected Ethernet service paths. The document defines the term Eth-LSP for an Ethernet service path that is controlled via GMPLS. Like all GMPLS-controlled services, such paths can use the common traffic engineering attributes: a bandwidth profile, a forwarding priority level, connection preemption characteristics, protection and resiliency capability, routing policy such as an explicit route, a bidirectional service, end-to-end and segment protection, and hierarchy. The bandwidth profile may set the committed information rate, the peak information rate and policies based on under- or over-subscription, and the services use a traffic specification that follows the Ethernet traffic parameters.

Applying GMPLS to transport Ethernet needs extensions, because the different service types have different forwarding functions. In general the header fields used in the forwarding function, such as the VLAN identifier and the destination MAC address, can be characterised as a data-plane label. In some circumstances these fields are constant along the path, and in others they vary hop by hop or at certain interfaces only. Where the labels must be forwarded unchanged, there are constraints on label allocation similar to those for other technologies such as lambda labels.

The characteristics of the transport Ethernet data plane are not modified in order to apply GMPLS control. In the IEEE 802.1Q data plane, for example, the VLAN identifier acts as a filter pointing to a particular forwarding table, and if the destination MAC address is found there the forwarding decision is made on that address. When forwarding using a spanning tree, if the destination address is not found, the frame is broadcast over all outgoing interfaces for which that identifier is defined, which is what supports Ethernet learning. A special case is when an identifier is defined for only two ports on one bridge, giving a point-to-point forwarding constraint, in which case all frames tagged with that identifier and received on one of those ports are forwarded out the other port without address learning. IEEE 802.1Qay allows learning to be turned off, and with it the broadcast mechanism that provides a way to create explicitly routed Ethernet connections.

The document does not define any specific format for an Eth-LSP label. Service-specific documents are expected to define the signalling and routing extensions needed for a given Ethernet service, and it is expected that a key requirement for them will be to describe label formats and encodings. It may also be necessary to provide a way to identify the required Ethernet service type in signalling and a way to advertise the capabilities of Ethernet switches in the routing protocols, so that requests for different paradigms, including new and existing ones, can be told apart. The switching type and the interface switching capability descriptor share a set of values that indicate what switching should and can be performed on a link for a path. Since the Layer-2 Switch Capable type may already be used by implementations doing Layer 2 switching, and to distinguish the different Ethernet switching paradigms, a new switching type needs to be defined for each new Ethernet switching paradigm supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The Ethernet frame fields used for forwarding become the label that GMPLS reserves and signals. Different Ethernet services use different fields, so each needs its own switching type value, and the actual label format is left to later documents.

sections.title: Routing, Signalling, Link Management and Path Computation
sections.content:
The GMPLS routing and addressing model is not modified. Control of Eth-LSPs uses the model of RFC 3945, most notably the use of IP addresses to identify interfaces and path end points, with support for both numbered and unnumbered interfaces. Where another address family or type of identifier is needed for an Ethernet service, extensions may be defined to map to an IP address, and support is expected to comply strictly with the GMPLS protocol suite addressing of RFC 3471 and RFC 3473.

GMPLS routing uses IP routing protocols with opaque type-length-value extensions to distribute traffic engineering information about routers and links, and that information is populated from resource information obtained by the Link Management Protocol or from configuration. The bandwidth resources of the links are tracked as paths are set up, and interfaces that support switching of Eth-LSPs are identified with the appropriate interface switching capability descriptor. New descriptors are expected to be defined for Eth-LSPs, and the Layer-2 Switch Capable descriptors will not be used for the interfaces defined here. GMPLS routing is optional, but it is valuable for maintaining topology and distributing the traffic engineering database used for path management and dynamic path computation.

For the control plane to operate, IP connectivity of sufficient capacity for the information exchange of the routing and signalling protocols is needed. One way is an IP-routed network with an interior gateway protocol that views each switch as a terminated IP adjacency, which gives IP traffic and a simple routing table for the control plane without requiring a high-performance IP data plane or forwarding user traffic over it. That IP connectivity can be provided as a separate independent network, out of band, or integrated with the Ethernet switches, in band.

GMPLS signalling is well suited to the control of Eth-LSPs and Ethernet switches. It can dynamically establish a path from an ingress node to an egress node; the signalled path may be completely static for its whole life, or signalling can adjust it in a coordinated fashion once established, and the choice between static and dynamic is under operator control. Standardised signalling also improves multi-vendor interoperability. Signalling supports both bidirectional and unidirectional data paths. Ethernet is bidirectional by nature and Connectivity Fault Management was built to use that, and before it the emulation of a physical wire and the learning requirements also mandated bidirectional connections, so Eth-LSPs need to be bidirectional congruent. They may be point-to-point or point-to-multipoint, and signalling allows full and partial protection.

On link management, link discovery for links interconnecting IEEE 802.1 bridges is specified in IEEE 802.1AB. Running it in large systems reduces configuration, reduces the chance of undetected configuration errors and exposes misconnections, but it is an optional feature and is not necessarily running before a link is operational, and it mainly supports the management plane. The Link Management Protocol has been defined for GMPLS control-plane link management and discovery, supports the automated creation of unnumbered interfaces for the control plane, and can support optional fault management. Without it there is extra configuration work for GMPLS link identifiers, and for large-scale implementations it is beneficial. With the newer Connectivity Fault Management and ITU-T capabilities, that optional fault management may not be needed. The goal is to let the user pick the best tool set, and the full functionality of Ethernet Connectivity Fault Management should be supported when a GMPLS control plane is used. The document expects the Link Management Protocol to be used for control-plane functions such as link property correlation, and Ethernet mechanisms for operations, such as Connectivity Fault Management and link trace, to be used for data-plane fault management and fault tracing.

GMPLS does not identify a specific method for selecting paths or supporting path computation, and allows a wide range, from very simple computation to elaborate coordination. Computation can be fully distributed, or done on a management station with local computation for rerouting, or on more sophisticated path computation servers. Eth-LSPs may use any path selection or computation mechanism, and the selection process should take into account the switching capabilities and encoding advertised for a particular interface. The emerging path computation element and selection work may also be used.

Finally, the document allows the signalling of Ethernet parameters across multiple VLANs, supporting both contiguous and hierarchical Ethernet paths, with the intention of reusing the GMPLS hierarchy for peer-to-peer models, user-network interfaces and network-network interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing, signalling, link management and path computation all come from GMPLS and are used as they are. The Ethernet-specific work is in the switching capability values and in the label format, which other documents will define.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A GMPLS-controlled transport Ethernet system should assume that users and devices attached to the user-network interfaces may behave maliciously, negligently or incorrectly. Intra-provider control traffic is trusted not to be malicious. In general these requirements are no different from the security requirements for operating any GMPLS network, and access to the trusted network happens only through the protocols defined for the user or network interface, or through protected management interfaces.

When in-band signalling is used for the control plane, the security of the control plane and the data plane may affect each other. With out-of-band signalling the data plane's security is decoupled from the control plane, so it has less impact on the overall security of the system.

Where GMPLS is applied to the control of the VLAN only, the commonly known techniques for mitigating Ethernet denial-of-service attacks may be required on the user-network interface ports.

For a fuller discussion the document points to the MPLS and GMPLS Security Framework, and notes that cryptography can protect against many of the attacks it describes. One option for protecting transport Ethernet is IEEE 802.1AE Media Access Control Security, which provides encryption and authentication. It is expected that solution documents will include a full analysis of the security issues any protocol extensions introduce.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone plugged into a customer port is assumed to be untrustworthy, so the provider's own control traffic has to be kept separate from it. Running the signalling out of band keeps a compromise of the data plane away from the control plane.

children.label: Port based
children.note: No service VLAN tagging and no MAC-address-based switching

children.label: one-to-one
children.note: Each VLAN identifier maps into a different service

children.label: many-to-one
children.note: Several identifiers map into the same service

children.label: all-to-one
children.note: All identifiers map into the same service; transparent maps one incoming port to one destination port

children.label: I-tagged
children.note: Uses a 24-bit service identifier carried in the I-TAG

items.title: Routing
items.text: Distributes the traffic engineering database, with interface switching capability descriptors identifying which interfaces can carry which kind of path.

items.title: Signalling
items.text: Establishes the path and can adjust it afterwards; the choice between a static path and a dynamic one is the operator's.

items.title: Link management
items.text: Discovers links and correlates their properties, and can create unnumbered control-plane interfaces automatically.

items.title: Path computation
items.text: May be distributed, done on a management station, or done by a path computation server; it is not fixed by GMPLS.
